subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Tourette syndrome and intermittent explosive disorder
vignette: A 12-year-old boy has sudden, repetitive facial grimacing, shoulder shrugging, and throat-clearing sounds for the past 2 years. The movements are nonrhythmic and he cannot suppress them for long. He also has intrusive thoughts about contamination and checks locks repeatedly. His teacher notes he is easily distracted and fidgety. He is otherwise healthy with a normal neurologic examination.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this boy's condition?

options.text: Onset after age 18 with vocal tics lasting less than 1 month
Recurrent outbursts of aggression lasting under 30 minutes with remorse
Multiple motor and vocal tics persisting over a year, associated with OCD and ADHD
A repetitive pattern of theft and destruction of property
Refusal to speak in certain situations despite normal speech at home

explanation_correct: Tourette syndrome has onset before age 18 and involves sudden, recurrent, nonrhythmic, stereotyped motor and vocal tics persisting for more than 1 year. Coprolalia (involuntary obscene speech) occurs in some patients. It is associated with OCD and ADHD, both of which this boy shows. Treatment is psychoeducation and behavioral therapy, with tetrabenazine, antipsychotics, or alpha-2 agonists for intractable, distressing tics.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tourette syndrome begins before age 18 and requires tics persisting for more than 1 year, not less than 1 month with adult onset.
explanation_incorrect.B: Brief aggressive outbursts with remorse describe intermittent explosive disorder, not the chronic motor and vocal tics seen here.
explanation_incorrect.D: A repetitive pattern of theft and property destruction describes conduct disorder, not a tic disorder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Refusing to speak in certain situations despite speaking elsewhere describes selective mutism, an anxiety disorder, not Tourette syndrome.

educationalObjective: Tourette syndrome features multiple motor and vocal tics lasting over a year with onset before 18, and is associated with OCD and ADHD.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Tourette syndrome and intermittent explosive disorder
vignette: A 19-year-old man reports sudden episodes in which he impulsively yells, throws objects, and sometimes strikes others when mildly provoked. Each episode lasts about 15 minutes, is out of proportion to the trigger, and is not planned. He describes an immediate sense of relief during the outburst followed by marked remorse afterward. The episodes have led to legal and social consequences. Onset was at age 10.
question: Which of the following features is most characteristic of intermittent explosive disorder?

options.text: Chronic irritability between discrete episodes with severe temper tantrums
Premeditated aggression toward people or animals with destruction of property
Sudden nonrhythmic motor and vocal tics persisting longer than a year
Brief, unpremeditated outbursts out of proportion to provocation with relief then remorse
Intentional fabrication of symptoms to assume the sick role

explanation_correct: Intermittent explosive disorder has onset after age 6 and involves recurrent verbal or physical outbursts representing failure to control aggressive impulses. Outbursts last less than 30 minutes, are out of proportion to provocation, are not premeditated, and may provide immediate relief followed by remorse; they can lead to legal, financial, or social consequences. Treatment includes psychotherapy and SSRIs.

explanation_incorrect.A: Chronic irritability between severe tantrums describes disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, not the discrete, brief episodes with remorse of intermittent explosive disorder.
explanation_incorrect.B: Premeditated aggression and property destruction suggest conduct disorder, whereas intermittent explosive outbursts are unplanned and brief.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sudden nonrhythmic motor and vocal tics lasting over a year describe Tourette syndrome, not an aggressive impulse-control disorder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Intentional fabrication of symptoms to assume the sick role describes factitious disorder, not intermittent explosive disorder.

educationalObjective: Intermittent explosive disorder features brief (<30 min), unpremeditated aggressive outbursts out of proportion to provocation with relief then remorse.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Tourette syndrome and intermittent explosive disorder
vignette: A 15-year-old boy with Tourette syndrome has multiple motor and vocal tics that have persisted for 3 years. They cause significant social distress and embarrassment but he has no other medical problems. His physician has tried psychoeducation and behavioral therapy without sufficient benefit, and the tics remain severe and distressing.
question: Which of the following pharmacologic options is appropriate for intractable, distressing tics in Tourette syndrome?

options.text: Tetrabenazine
Methylphenidate
Lithium
Fluoxetine
Atomoxetine

explanation_correct: For intractable and distressing tics in Tourette syndrome, treatment options include tetrabenazine, antipsychotics, and alpha-2 agonists. Initial management is psychoeducation and behavioral therapy. Coprolalia occurs in some patients but is not required for diagnosis, and the disorder is associated with OCD and ADHD.

explanation_incorrect.B: Methylphenidate is a stimulant used for ADHD; while ADHD commonly coexists with Tourette, stimulants are not the treatment for tics themselves.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lithium is a mood stabilizer used in bipolar disorder, not for tics in Tourette syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fluoxetine is an SSRI used for depression, anxiety, and OCD, but it is not a primary treatment for the motor and vocal tics of Tourette syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atomoxetine is a nonstimulant treatment for ADHD, not for intractable tics in Tourette syndrome.

educationalObjective: Intractable, distressing Tourette tics can be treated with tetrabenazine, antipsychotics, or alpha-2 agonists after behavioral measures fail.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Tourette syndrome and intermittent explosive disorder
vignette: A 10-year-old boy randomly blurted out obscene words during class on several occasions, which he says he could not control. He also has repetitive blinking and shoulder jerking that has been present for 18 months. He feels embarrassed and distressed by the outbursts. His parents report he has always been particular about symmetry and order.
question: Which of the following best describes the involuntary obscene speech this boy exhibits?

options.text: A core feature of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
Coprolalia, which occurs in some patients with Tourette syndrome
A defining feature of intermittent explosive disorder
Factitious symptoms produced intentionally for secondary gain
A language regression consistent with autism spectrum disorder

explanation_correct: Coprolalia is involuntary obscene speech and is found in some patients with Tourette syndrome, though it is not required for diagnosis. This boy's multiple motor tics (blinking, shoulder jerking) lasting more than a year with onset before 18 support the diagnosis. Tourette is associated with OCD features such as his preoccupation with symmetry and order.

explanation_incorrect.A: ADHD involves inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, not involuntary obscene speech and tics, although it commonly coexists with Tourette syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intermittent explosive disorder involves aggressive outbursts with remorse, not the involuntary vocal tics of coprolalia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Factitious symptoms are intentionally produced for primary or secondary gain; coprolalia in Tourette syndrome is involuntary and not produced intentionally.
explanation_incorrect.E: Autism spectrum disorder involves early social/communication deficits and restricted behaviors, not the motor and vocal tics described here.

educationalObjective: Coprolalia is involuntary obscene speech seen in some Tourette syndrome patients, alongside motor and vocal tics persisting over a year.
